title: Magnetic Fields Produced by Currents: Ampere’s Law
lead: A current makes a magnetic field, and the shape the wire is wound in decides the shape of that field. This section gives the field of a long straight wire as $\kBmag = \mu_0\kIcur/2\pi\kr$, states right hand rule 2 for the direction of the circles it makes, and names the Biot-Savart law and Ampere’s law, which say that the field of a current of any shape is the sum of the fields of its segments. It then follows the same circular field around a flat loop, where the circles crowd together at the center, and down the inside of a solenoid, where they become the strong and uniform field an MRI magnet is made of.
objectives: Calculate current that produces a magnetic field.
Use the right hand rule 2 to determine the direction of current or the direction of magnetic field loops.
summary_html:
• The strength of the magnetic field created by current in a long straight wire is given by $\kBmag = \frac{\mu_0\kIcur}{2\pi\kr}(\text{long straight wire})$, where $\kIcur$ is the current, $\kr$ is the shortest distance to the wire, and the constant $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\;\text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}$ is the permeability of free space.
  • The direction of the magnetic field created by a long straight wire is given by right hand rule 2 (RHR-2): Point the thumb of the right hand in the direction of current, and the fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field loops created by it.
  • The magnetic field created by current following any path is the sum (or integral) of the fields due to segments along the path (magnitude and direction as for a straight wire), resulting in a general relationship between current and field known as Ampere’s law.
  • The magnetic field strength at the center of a circular loop is given by $\kBmag = \frac{\mu_0\kIcur}{2\kR} (\text{at center of loop})$, where $\kR$ is the radius of the loop. This equation becomes $\kBmag = \mu_0 n\kIcur/(2\kR)$ for a flat coil of $N$ loops. RHR-2 gives the direction of the field about the loop. A long coil is called a solenoid.
  • The magnetic field strength inside a solenoid is $\kBmag = \mu_0 n\kIcur\;\;(\text{inside a solenoid})$, where $n$ is the number of loops per unit length of the solenoid. The field inside is very uniform in magnitude and direction.

exercises.prompt: An experimentalist fires a beam of electrons, creating a visible path in the air that can be measured. The beam is fired along a direction parallel to a current-carrying wire, and the electrons travel in a circular path in response to the wire’s magnetic field. Assuming the mass and charge of the electrons is known, what quantities would you need to measure in order to deduce the current in the wire?

options: the radius of the circular path
the average distance between the electrons and the wire
answer.hint: Write down the two relations the situation obeys, the radius of the circle a charge makes in a field and the field a long straight wire makes at a given distance, and then see which symbols are still unknown once the mass and the charge of the electron are given.

exercises.prompt: Electrons starting from rest are accelerated through a potential difference of 240 V and fired into a region of uniform 3.5-mT magnetic field generated by a large solenoid. The electrons are initially moving in the +x-direction upon entering the field, and the field is directed into the page. Determine (a) the radius of the circle in which the electrons will move in this uniform magnetic field and (b) the initial direction of the magnetic force the electrons feel upon entering the uniform field of the solenoid.

answer.solution: Take the two steps in order. All the work the potential difference does on an electron becomes kinetic energy, so $\kqe\kV = \frac{1}{2}m_{\text{e}}\kv^2$ and the speed on entering the field is $\kv = \sqrt{2\kqe\kV/m_{\text{e}}} = \sqrt{2(1.60\times10^{-19}\ \text{C})(240\ \text{V})/(9.11\times10^{-31}\ \text{kg})} = 9.2\times10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$. (a) Inside the solenoid the field is uniform and the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the path is a circle whose radius is $\kr = m_{\text{e}}\kv/\kqe\kBmag = (9.11\times10^{-31}\ \text{kg})(9.2\times10^{6}\ \text{m/s})/[(1.60\times10^{-19}\ \text{C})(3.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{T})] = 1.5\times10^{-2}\ \text{m}$, or about 15 mm. (b) Point the thumb of your right hand in the $+x$-direction along the velocity and your fingers into the page along the field: your palm pushes toward the top of the page, which is the direction of the force a positive charge would feel there. An electron carries a negative charge, so it is pushed the other way, toward the bottom of the page, in the $-y$-direction.

exercises.prompt:
In terms of the direction of force, we use the left-hand rule. Pointing your thumb in the +x-direction with the velocity and fingers of the left hand into the page reveals that the magnetic force points down toward the bottom of the page in the –y-direction.

A wire along the y-axis carries current in the +y-direction. In what direction is the magnetic field at a point on the +x-axis near the wire?

answer.hint: The field of a straight wire does not point away from the wire; it circles it. Point the thumb of your right hand along the current and see which way your fingers pass through a point out on the $+x$-axis.

exercises.prompt: Imagine the xy coordinate plane is the plane of the page. A wire along the z-axis carries current in the +z-direction (out of the page, or $\odot$). Draw a diagram of the magnetic field in the vicinity of this wire indicating the direction of the field. Also, describe how the strength of the magnetic field varies according to the distance from the z-axis.

answer.solution: The wire comes straight out of the page at the origin, so point the thumb of your right hand out of the page along the current and your fingers curl counterclockwise. The field lines are therefore circles centered on the origin, drawn counterclockwise: at a point on the $+x$-axis the field points in the $+y$-direction, at a point on the $+y$-axis it points in the $-x$-direction, and so on all the way round. Draw several of those circles at increasing distances from the origin, put an arrow on each to carry the counterclockwise sense, and note that the field at any point is tangent to the circle through it rather than directed away from the wire. For the strength, the field of a long straight wire is $\kBmag = \mu_0\kIcur/2\pi\kr$, so it is inversely proportional to the distance $\kr$ from the $z$-axis: doubling the distance halves the field, and tripling it leaves a third. The circles you draw should carry shorter arrows the farther out they are, and none of them should be drawn at the origin itself, where the formula for a long straight wire no longer applies.

exercises.prompt: Make a drawing and use RHR-2 to find the direction of the magnetic field of a current loop in a motor (such as in Figure 22.33). Then show that the direction of the torque on the loop is the same as produced by like poles repelling and unlike poles attracting.

answer.solution: Draw the loop of the motor between the poles of the permanent magnet, with the field of the magnet running across the page from its north pole to its south pole, and mark which way the current goes round the loop. Now apply RHR-2 to the loop itself: point the thumb of your right hand along the current in one side of the loop and your fingers curl the way that side’s field goes, and doing this all the way round shows that the loop’s own field comes out of one face of the loop and goes in at the other. The loop is therefore a small magnet, with its north pole on the face the field leaves by and its south pole on the other. Now compare the two magnets. In any position except the face-on one, the loop’s north pole is turned partly toward the north pole of the permanent magnet and its south pole partly toward that magnet’s south pole. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract, so the loop is pushed round until its north pole faces the magnet’s south pole, and there, face-on, the pushing and the pulling are balanced and the turning stops. That is exactly the sense the torque $\ktau = N\kIcur A\kBmag\sin\theta$ gives: it is largest when the loop is side-on to the field, falls to zero when the loop is face-on, and always acts to bring the loop face-on. The two accounts are one account, because the loop’s poles are made by its own current.
